label: Conflict at Work
framing: The workplace is where most of us spend our days under people we did not choose, and Scripture has more to say about it than we expect. It treats your work as worship and your conduct toward a hard boss or a scheming colleague as a real test of the faith you carry past the church door.
cultural: Our culture splits the self in two, a spiritual life for Sunday and a professional life governed by whatever it takes, so that conflict at work feels like a place where faith simply does not apply. The ancient world ran on patronage, rivalry, and the climb, much as ours does. Scripture refuses the split, insisting that the God you serve on Sunday is the same one watching how you treat the coworker who undercut you on Monday.
historical: Paul wrote to slaves and masters in the first century about working as for the Lord and not for men, words that reshaped how the church understood ordinary labor. The Reformers recovered the dignity of common work as a calling, Luther teaching that the milkmaid and the magistrate served God in their stations, and the long tradition since has held that integrity under an unjust authority is among the quietest and hardest forms of witness.
application: Address the conflict directly and privately first, rather than building a faction or rehearsing your case to everyone but the person involved. Do your work with such integrity that the accusation finds nothing to land on. Refuse the easy weapons, the gossip, the sabotage, the withheld effort, even when they are used against you. And entrust the outcome, the promotion, the vindication, the unfair boss, to a God who sees what no performance review records.

verses.text: Thus the administrators and satraps sought a charge against Daniel concerning the kingdom, but they could find no charge or corruption, because he was trustworthy, and no negligence or corruption was found in him. Finally these men said, “We will never find any charge against this Daniel, unless we find something against him concerning the law of his God.”
verses.where: Daniel's fellow officials look for a charge against him and can find no corruption or negligence, because he is trustworthy. The site's note on the chapter says it was jealousy at his rise that set them plotting. Their only hope, they decide, is something to do with his faith, and the integrity of his work leaves them nothing else.

verses.text: But he refused. “Look,” he said to his master’s wife, “with me here, my master does not concern himself with anything in his house, and he has entrusted everything he owns to my care. No one in this house is greater than I am. He has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. So how could I do such a great evil and sin against God?” Although Potiphar’s wife spoke to Joseph day after day, he refused to go to bed with her or even be near her.
verses.where: Joseph, managing his master's house, refuses the advances of his master's wife day after day, and will not even be near her. The site's plain note says he said no again and again to someone who had power over him, and on the verses that follow it says that anyone pressured by a boss or anyone with power over them is not to blame, and that saying no is right even if they punish you for it. Joseph's refusal cost him his post.

verses.text: So Abram said to Lot, “Please let there be no contention between you and me, or between your herdsmen and my herdsmen. After all, we are brothers. Is not the whole land before you? Now separate yourself from me. If you go to the left, I will go to the right; if you go to the right, I will go to the left.”
verses.where: The herdsmen of Abram and Lot quarrel because the land cannot hold both households, and Abram asks that there be no contention between them and offers Lot first choice. The site's note says the problem was not hostility but abundance, and that Abram appealed to kinship rather than his rank as the elder. The one with the right to choose first gave it away to keep the peace.

verses.text: Their disagreement was so sharp that they parted company. Barnabas took Mark and sailed for Cyprus, but Paul chose Silas and left, commended by the brothers to the grace of the Lord.
verses.where: Paul and Barnabas disagree so sharply over taking Mark that they part company and go to different places. The site's plain note says Luke does not hide that two faithful men quarrelled, and that God kept working through both of them. Not every conflict between good colleagues ends in agreement, and a parting is not always a failure.

verses.text: I urge Euodia and Syntyche to agree with each other in the Lord. Yes, and I ask you, my true yokefellow, to help these women who have labored with me for the gospel, along with Clement and the rest of my fellow workers, whose names are in the Book of Life.
verses.where: Paul pleads with two women who had laboured beside him for the gospel to agree with each other in the Lord, and asks a true yokefellow to help them. The site's plain note says Paul names the quarrel but takes no side, and asks whether you could be the one who helps two people at odds. Fellow workers falling out is as old as the church's own work.

verses.text: There is an evil I have seen under the sun— an error that proceeds from the ruler: Folly is appointed to great heights, but the rich sit in lowly positions. I have seen slaves on horseback, while princes go on foot like slaves.
verses.where: The Teacher has seen an error that proceeds from the ruler: folly set in high places while the able sit low. The site's note on the chapter puts it plainly, that fools are promoted while the capable are passed over. Scripture does not pretend that promotion always follows merit.

verses.text: And Saul was furious and resented this song. “They have ascribed tens of thousands to David,” he said, “but only thousands to me. What more can he have but the kingdom?” And from that day forward Saul kept a jealous eye on David.
verses.where: When the women's song credits David with tens of thousands and Saul with thousands, Saul is furious and keeps a jealous eye on David from that day. The site's note on the chapter says the song turned Saul's admiration into jealousy, and that he twice tried to spear David. David served a jealous superior for a time, and when the spear came he got out of its way, as verse 11 says.

verses.text: If your brother sins against you, go and confront him privately. If he listens to you, you have won your brother over.
verses.where: Jesus says that if a brother sins against you, go to him privately, and if he listens you have won him over. The site's plain note says he sends you to the person, not to everyone else about the person, and that these steps are for wrongs between people on roughly equal ground; they do not fit a case where one person has power over another or where someone is afraid. Abuse and crimes go to the proper authorities.

verses.text: Then some soldiers asked him, “And what should we do?” “Do not take money by force or false accusation,” he said. “Be content with your wages.”
verses.where: Soldiers ask John the Baptist what they should do, and he tells them not to take money by force or false accusation and to be content with their wages. The site's note says John does not tell them to leave their service but to stop abusing its power, each group hearing the temptation of its own trade. False accusation is named among the sins of a working life.

verses.text: And masters, do the same for your slaves. Give up your use of threats, because you know that He who is both their Master and yours is in heaven, and there is no favoritism with Him.
verses.where: Paul tells masters to give up their use of threats, because master and servant share one Master in heaven who shows no favoritism. The site's plain note says a worker is not property and a boss is not an owner, that treating workers without threats can be applied to work with care, and that no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work. It asks anyone with power over others whether they use threats, open or quiet.

misread.taken: Servants, submit to your masters, even to those who are unreasonable is used to tell a worker who is being bullied, harassed or threatened that a Christian should stay quiet and put up with it.
misread.says: The site's plain note says Peter writes to slaves with no way out, in an empire that crushed slave revolts, and that within that world he calls their unjust treatment unjust and sets them beside Christ. It says the passage is never a reason to tell someone who is being hurt by another person that they must stay and bear it, and that nothing in it asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. The note on Ephesians 6 adds that a worker is not property and a boss is not an owner.
misread.text: Servants, submit yourselves to your masters with all respect, not only to those who are good and gentle, but even to those who are unreasonable. For if anyone endures the pain of unjust suffering because he is conscious of God, this is to be commended.

whole: If someone at work is threatening you, pressuring you for sex, or hurting you, that is not an ordinary conflict, and you do not have to manage it alone: tell someone you trust and get help, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Most conflict at work is less dramatic and still wears people down. A colleague takes credit for your work. A manager plays favourites, or loses their temper in meetings, or never says anything directly. Two departments are at war and everyone is expected to take a side. The promotion goes to someone else. Because work pays the bills, it can feel impossible to say anything, and so the conflict is carried home and replayed at night.

Scripture recognizes all of it. Daniel's colleagues plotted against him out of jealousy. Saul grew jealous of David the day a song praised him more. The Teacher saw fools promoted while capable people sat low. Paul and Barnabas, two good men, disagreed so sharply that they parted, and two women who had worked beside Paul fell out badly enough for him to name them in a letter. Beneath much conflict at work the Bible sees the same things it sees everywhere: rivalry, fear of losing face, and the abuse of power by those who have it over others. It also sees how easily the one who is wronged picks up the same weapons, the gossip, the faction, the quiet sabotage.

So the Bible's wisdom is practical and does not ask for silence about wrong. Where it is safe and the two of you stand on roughly equal ground, go to the person and not to everyone else about them, as Jesus says. Do your work so faithfully that, as with Daniel, an accusation has nothing to land on. Give up the right to win every point, as Abram gave Lot first choice to end the quarrel. Ask someone to help, as Paul asked his true yokefellow to help Euodia and Syntyche. Where the conflict is a person with power using it badly, the steps of Matthew 18 do not fit, and the notes say so; use the proper channels at work and seek advice. If you are the one with power, hear Paul's word to masters: give up threats, for you have a Master too.

The hope Scripture gives is that the God who sees behind every closed door is the judge of every workplace. Joseph lost his post for doing right, and the LORD was with him in the prison. Paul and Barnabas parted, and God worked through both. Your reputation, your promotion and your vindication do not finally rest with a manager or a review. You can do honest work, refuse the easy weapons, speak up where wrong is done, and leave the rest to the one who shows no favoritism.
deep.sit: Is there someone at work you have talked about more than you have talked to, and is it safe to go to them?

prayer.lead: The site's plain note says the songs of ascents begin in a place of lies and conflict, among people who want war when you want peace, and that this psalm lets you say so to God. Pray it before a hard day at work.
prayer.text: In my distress I cried to the LORD, and He answered me. Deliver my soul, O LORD, from lying lips and a deceitful tongue.

careLines.text: Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help.
You are not to blame for their pressure.
But no one should use these verses to demand silence about mistreatment at work.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
